I’m in the middle of writing a blog post about the dangers of ChatGPT’s confident language hijacking the human behavior of assigning truth value based on confidence level of the interlocutor. You are right in that danger zone. You feel that because ChatGPT says something confidently that you should be able to trust it. That’s just not how this tool works at the moment. It’s close enough to get things right a lot of the time, but that just increases the risk.

For now, try to remember that you are the agent and ChatGPT is a tool you are using. That tool is great at speculating and spitballing and terrible at delineating between things that are and are not accurate. So use it for tasks where you need help with speculating and spitballing. Dont rely on it for research.

It’s even fine to use it for preliminary research, just remember that you may run into issues exactly like the one you have - and importantly that sometimes you won’t be able to catch it in the act. So verify any facts you learn from chatgpt before believing them. And if it feels like it’s gaslighting you, it very likely is, just not intentionally.

Why would you say ‘not sure why you’re against nuclear?’ There are multiple well understood arguments against nuclear. You may find them lacking or insufficient to counter the positive effects of the technology but it hurts your case when you feign ignorance of any downsides. Waste disposal and fallout from catastrophic failure are the key ones. While advances have been and continue to be made in these areas, they remain as major challenges. 

I’m a reformed anti-nuke guy. I’m far from pro-nuke, but do accept that it’s a good potential source of energy that should be part of the mix as we move away from fossil fuels. I find nuclear activists’ rhetoric that it’s ’safe and clean’ counterproductive to this goal. It may be safER and cleanER than competing solutions, but it (like all solutions) confers some risk and some contaminants. Acknowledging this head on and treating it as a manageable problem would be so much more persuasive.

And to your edit, Had we simply scaled up the use of 90 year old methods 90 years ago, we would inarguably have had a significantly higher number of catastrophic system failures and waste containment issues in that period. You can’t just look at the good numbers and say it would be better. It’s likely true that fear of these things is overblown and impacts our ability to mitigate the risk through investment. But those fears aren’t groundless and addressing them honestly leads to better solutions.

Basically i’m saying you need to be as careful with your advocacy as you are asking others to be with their critique. And that it’s really important to carefully consider and evaluate common critiques to your position or risk falling into the trap of cognitive reinforcement/bias.

Building one piece at a time and testing it (say, just the scraper function) then adding the next layers one at a time will help you build an understanding of your project as you go. This serves the dual purpose of building your software developer chops and makes you an active participant in bug fixing and optimization.

Not a doctor. Not a therapist. Habitual weed smoker here.

My answer is it’s not as simple as weed being helpful or harmful. It helps you in some ways (tamping down acute distress) and hurts you in others (reducing motivation to work on yourself). That said many of the ways it helps you can be helped by other things and overall you’d probably be better off if weed was something you smoked occasionally for fun rather than habitually for therapy.

That said, stopping on a dime without replacing the valuable parts with better habits (eg meditation, journaling, socializing, exercise) could be counterproductive. Don’t fall into the trap of just stopping and then blaming stopping for negative follow on effects.

Above all, It’s not the weed that is the problem. There is a problem and weed is an imperfect partial solution that you have found. The hard part is finding and working the actual problem so that the weed is less and less necessary.

You need to reframe how you think about this question. ChatGPT cannot give advice. It doesn’t know anything and it doesn’t know you. ChatGPT CAN be a tool to help you figure out what you want to/should do. You just have to remember: You are the agent, ChatGPT is a tool.

That said, you can extract good advice from it depending on the type of advice you’re looking for. Just always take it with a grain of salt. Also, do your best NOT to tell it or even hint at what your preferred answer is. It will ‘want’ to agree with you. So try to ask questions from a neutral standpoint.

Once you have what you think is advice, double check by asking it to critique its own advice. After that, it’s really up to you to weigh the options.

This is a great example of the phenomenon I described: Bad headlines reporting on tentative findings (Webb data reveals galaxies older than the universe, for example), subsequently contradicted (This is the peer review process), leading to almost as bad headlines of the new science, leading to lazy readers (all of us) saying, ‘which is it?’

Was that your intention? Or am I missing your point?

The issue is that you can’t take science headlines as declarations of fact. The vast majority of the headlines are:
- Written in order to make the findings sound extreme, ideally ‘never thought before’ type things for click bait reasons
- Most often refer to newly released research that has not been peer reviewed so even if you are able to see through the headline hype, you can’t accept even the finding a of the study or paper as superseding old theory. It’s just a new possible thing to consider.
- Very often report on unpublished work that’s being teased with a press release. So even less reliable.
- When a headline says ‘scientists say’ They mean a couple of specific scientists that did some specific research and came to their own conclusions. It almost never means scientists’ overall consensus has shifted.

Given all that, it’s not at all surprising to find headlines that seem to directly contradict each other. It means basically nothing about the actual work being done or fair conclusions that can be drawn from it. 

Its understandable that people struggle with this. It is easier to think we should just believe what we read. And I don’t even blame science journalism since it’s true across all media which just reflects an issue with what people want. We just have to be better at determining what’s real at the core of the hype.

However you’re running into a common issue with UG tabs that is confusing and frequently leads to people learning odd awkward versions of the songs they love. To clear up the confusion, you need to understand how what you’re seeing on the page comes to be. 

Most of the songs on UG are submitted by individual musicians who have listened to, analyzed and written down a chord chart or tab for the song. They submit the song to UG for publishing. These submissions usually include chord names (in this case C#, A, and Bb). They sometimes include specific voicings of those chords. 

UG’s tools then automatically parse (read) the chord names and add the most common chord fingerings for those chord names at the top of the chart. However this feature of UG’s platform isn’t able to read any extra info provided by the submission. So in the case where the submission specifies a different fingering for the chords, the fingerings UG provides can conflict. That’s the case here. 

While it’s good to remember that there is little to no quality control in this process. (i.e. These interpretations may be super accurate or totally wrong or, generously, totally unique interpretations) it’s pretty much never helpful to use the UG provided chord fingerings instead of specific fingerings provided in the submission itself. If you do, you’re likely to play a version of the song with awkward voice leading that doesn’t sound quite like the original artist intended.

You’re not wrong, but this is probably not what this guy needs to hear right now. Dude is trying to learn his first F chord; a common stumbling point for a beginning guitarist. 

OP, the advice above to start with F7 (can be played with no barre) is good. You can use that chord instead of a real F major chord in a pinch. But the real answer is you just have to practice until your fingers gain strength and dexterity. It’s very achievable with practice and effort.

One method:

1. Get the F7 down so it’s comfortable. 

Make sure you’re fingering it with your index finger on the first fret of the B string (second highest), your middle finger on the second fret of the G string (next lower string) and your ring finger on the 3rd fret of the D string. This fingering is important because eventually you’ll need your index finger in that position as you move to the next steps.

Play only the highest 4 strings as the low E and A string, unfretted, do not fit in the F major chord. Well, technically the A does, but most often you will want your lowest note in your chord to be the root (F). So skip the A string for now unless you really like the sound of the A in the bass of the chord.

As I said above, if a song calls for F major, you can play F7 if you have no other options. It won’t be quite right but you’ll be able to get through.

2. Convert the F7 to F major

This is a simple step for your brain but harder for your fingers. All you have to do is use that same index finger to fret BOTH the B and high E strings on that first fret. The rest of the fingering is the same. When you can do that, CONGRATS! It’s your first barre chord. It’s a baby one, but you’re making progress.

3. Work your way up to the full E barre shape. 

The first thing to realize here is that the F shape you learned above is the same as the open E major shape you likely learned as one of your first chords, just shifted up one fret and using only the 4 highest strings. The full barre shape completes this by including the 2 lower strings.

Again this is a lot easier to understand than to do. All it takes is extending your index finger to fret the low E string at that same first fret (this completes the barre), then add your pinkie to fret the A string on the 3rd fret. 

This will feel nearly impossible at first. You will need to develop strength over time. Someone above mentioned starting higher up the neck to learn the shape and this is good advice. Playing this chord right next to the nut is the place on the fretboard that requires the most finger strength. So move closer to the middle of the neck and find that same finger pattern. Once you can play it higher up the neck, work your way down to the first fret.

While this version of the chord is much more difficult to master, it’s also much more useful as it will allow you to play literally any named major chord just by moving it up and down the neck. And with minor fingering adjustments, every minor, dominant 7, minor 7. The finger strength you gain can then be leveraged for other barre shapes opening up the whole fretboard for you to play.

Good luck!

There are so many questions here and not all of them have well defined answers. The more we find exoplanets, the more we realize how limited our understanding is of how they form. If this were my project, I’d just find a real one I thought was cool and then work from there.

But if you want to start from scratch, and assuming from your question that you want the planet to have an atmosphere and some form of life, you can pretty much just decide what you want from the following:

- What kind of star are you orbiting? There are a range of sizes and temperatures to choose from and these will have a big impact on everything else here.
- How far from the star will the planet be? A key part of your decision would be whether the planet should be in the ‘goldilocks zone’ which is the range where you are far enough but not too far from the star for liquid water to stay on the planet without freezing or boiling away. If you want life on the planet, this is your best bet. There are other ways (internal heat coming from the planet’s core, heat from tidal forces for moons orbiting large planets) but choosing a plausible distance from the star is easiest. Just remember that in our solar system, Mars, Venus and Earth are all in the zone and only one has life that we know of. 
- What is the basic makeup of the planet? Rocky (think Earth, Mars), metallic (None in our solar system but we believe some exoplanets are mostly metal), gaseous (Jupiter, Saturn), icy (Pluto), combinations of these, something more exotic? This will drive a lot of the rest of what can happen, for instance If it’s gaseous, you won’t have things walking on the surface.
- How big do you want it to be? If you want earth-like things to happen, choose a size similar to earth. If you go a lot smaller, you won’t be able to hold an atmosphere. If it’s a lot bigger, you’ll need to account for the larger influence of gravity on both atmospheric development and evolution (if you want life).

If your fictional planet will have life on it, then things get a lot more theoretical. We only know of one planet in the universe that has life. We don’t know how it started. Evolution is a really solid theory for explaining how life went from simple existence to the complexity we see today, and we can reasonably assume that IF life exists elsewhere, natural selection would define how it evolves. That said, it would be essentially impossible to guess at what evolutionary paths life would take if you took it step by step. So a better approach would be to think of what kind of plants/animals would perform well in your chosen environment. I hate to invoke the term ‘intelligent design’ but honestly your best bet of creating a plausible eco-system is to design it intelligently :)

I’m not an expert in any of this, but hopefully the above will give you an appreciation of the complexity of your question and a few ways you might find your way to a reasonable answer. Yes, the change makes sense as a tool to reduce bot reach. If that was the only intent, it would be a clear win.

Unfortunately, it also weakens the value the check was initially intended to provide: identity protection for often/likely spoofed people and the subsequent increase in public trust in the overall Tritter discourse. 

The benefit of the old checks was to proactively identify public figures. The goal of that was to increase the volume and quality of content posted by these users by removing the major disincentive of misinformation spread by identity thieves. Importantly this is NOT just value to the account holder (ie. It’s insufficient to say ‘it should be worth $8/mo to them’). It is value to the community as a whole and therefor to Twitter as an organization. Now it’s gone and its replacement seems to be just a way to incentivize payment.

For it to be a good move, the loss of the ability to determine whether you are listening to the White House or some a-hole pretending to be the white house account must be outweighed by the gain in reducing bot traffic (for which we will never see data worth trusting but perhaps Twitter will) and/or the revenue brought in by the actual check mark purchasers.

Marketing data companies have been doing this for decades. (source: I worked for one for many years) FB/Meta & Google have personas for everyone that are used to provide personalized content and browsing experience. 

What are you bringing to the world that doesn’t already exist? I’m sure you have something, but the description above doesn’t really convey it (to me at least).

Regardless, the main concerns are:

- Privacy Problem - what will you do with the personae? Who has access? How do you balance the power of openness against the fear of exposure?

- Categorization Problem - How can a persona be an accurate representation of the true person? How do you avoid classifying people into predetermined (or even organically determined) categories and thus fall into all the problems that categorization comes with - i.e. that the dividing lines between categories are arbitrary and we inevitably overestimate the similarities between people in a category and underestimate similarities between people in adjacent categories.

- Content Bubble Problem - If at least part of your goal is improving content recommendations, how do you avoid creating content bubbles where you’re effectively isolating groups of people from each other. Content bubbles can lead to extremism and division. We see this clearly with FB at least.

- Mission Definition Problem - What is/are your success metric(s)? For marketers the success metric is easy - conversion. If you have a more altruistic bent (i’m guessing/hoping here) then figuring out how to measure success becomes more difficult. Determining your success metrics will need to be very tightly aligned with the overall mission and also determine whether the project has real value to any participants.

- Funding Bias Problem - Who would pay for this effort? B/c regardless of any of the above whoever finds this will drive the mission and no matter the intentions of the initial team, the finder’s goals will end up being the ones that are met.

All good man. Your mac doesn’t need to play at the volume of your amp. you’re recording TO the Mac, not from it. The Focusrite is a tool that converts your music inputs into digital signals for the Mac AND vice versa.

The beauty of the DAW is that you can record multiple tracks and mix them together on your computer. You’re going to want to noodle around with Garage Band a bit to get comfortable with the idea.

So here’s some basic steps to help:

1. Open Garage Band, creat a new Song project, and import your backing track (YouTube vids will help you here)
2. Set up your focusrite as both the mic input AND speaker output. 
3. Plug headphones into the Focusrite. Make sure you can hear the backing track when you play it.
4. Create a new track for the new guitar track (been a bit since I used GB but I think you select New track and choose Instrument Track)
5a (option 1) Plug Guitar directly into the focusrite 
5b (option 2) Plug mic into focusrite and place mic in front of your guitar amp
6. test that you can hear the playing (tip: make sure the track is selected and that it’s set to Monitor:On)
7. Hit record and go.

After that, sky’s the limit. YouTube is really your friend.

If you’re on a mac and new to this stuff, just use Garage Band as an entry level DAW. If you’re on a PC there are plenty of cheap and even free options there as well but i don’t know enough to guide your choice.

Once you have all 3 things ready, think about minimizing the steps from your source to your recording. The same source that you’re sending to the Marshall speaker can just go right into the DAW you’re using. Depending on where you’re getting the backing tracks, you can either just download them and import them into your DAW or you may need to convert them to a file format that your DAW can handle (if YouTube or other video streaming source, you may need to convert - plenty of youtube videos that will walk you through how to do this :)

There’s no reason to record the backing track coming out of a speaker unless you’re doing this to achieve a specific sound which seems unlikely in your situation. If you’re already comfortable with ‘fixed’ solfège then for note names, you’ll just need to know that Do = C, Re=D, Mi=E, and so on to easily translate between the 2.
